Shift register and PN code

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how a small shift register generates a repeatable sequence with a strong timing signature.

A receiver can search for a known pseudo-noise code in a weak signal. A linear feedback shift register updates binary state through XOR taps. With a primitive feedback polynomial and a nonzero five-bit seed, the maximal period is 2⁵−1 = 31 chips.

Correlation uses bipolar values, such as b[n] = 2c[n]−1. The ideal periodic autocorrelation of this m-sequence is 31 at zero shift and −1 at every nonzero cyclic shift. That distinction creates a recognizable code-phase peak.

This small sequence illustrates the mechanism. GPS C/A codes use two ten-stage registers combined into Gold-code sequences with a 1023-chip period; their cross-correlation and autocorrelation details differ from this five-stage example.

Example

The recurrence c[n+5] = c[n+2] XOR c[n] starts from 11111. After 31 chips it repeats the original state. A one-chip wrong cyclic alignment gives correlation −1 instead of 31 in the noiseless bipolar model.

    Practice

    1. Why must a maximal-length XOR register use a nonzero seed?

    Evaluate each XOR tap when all register bits are zero.

    The all-zero state maps to itself forever, so it cannot enter the nonzero maximal cycle.

    2. Why convert bits 0 and 1 into −1 and +1 before this correlation?

    Think about how agreements and disagreements should contribute.

    Matching chips contribute +1 and differing chips contribute −1. A raw 0/1 product would count coincident ones but would not give that symmetric agreement-minus-disagreement statistic.
